## Introduction

On Day 19, k-means with K = 3 put 88 colleges, including all four Claremont
Colleges, in one **elite** cluster. One cluster hides a lot: Harvard and
Harvey Mudd are both in it. A tree of all 88 is hard to read, so today we
take **30** of them: the four Claremont Colleges, 14 other liberal arts
colleges, and 12 research universities. We build a **tree** for those 30 and
look at the structure inside.

The chunk below uses Day 19's eight columns, standardized over all 777
colleges, and keeps the 30. `Z_elite` has one row per college, and its **row
names** are the college names, so they show up in the dendrogram.

**Estimated time: 25 minutes.** The goal for today is **Parts 1–3**. If you
finish them, keep going with the **Bonus** section at the end. If you don't
reach the Bonus, that's completely fine.

Each task ends with a question in *italics*. Write a sentence or two for each.

```{r load}
data(College)
colleges <- College %>%
  mutate(college = rownames(College),          # the names are row names; make them a column
         accept_rate = Accept / Apps) %>%      # share of applicants admitted
  select(college, Private, accept_rate, Top10perc, F.Undergrad, Outstate,
         S.F.Ratio, perc.alumni, Expend, Grad.Rate)

claremont <- c("Claremont McKenna College", "Harvey Mudd College",
               "Pitzer College", "Scripps College")
liberal_arts <- c("Amherst College", "Williams College", "Wellesley College",
                  "Bowdoin College", "Carleton College", "Davidson College",
                  "Reed College", "Occidental College", "Grinnell College",
                  "Macalester College", "Vassar College", "Barnard College",
                  "Bryn Mawr College", "Smith College")
universities <- c("Harvard University", "Yale University", "Princeton University",
                  "Massachusetts Institute of Technology", "Duke University",
                  "Columbia University", "Brown University", "Dartmouth College",
                  "University of Pennsylvania", "Northwestern University",
                  "University of California at Berkeley",
                  "University of Michigan at Ann Arbor")
picked <- c(claremont, liberal_arts, universities)

# Day 19: standardize the eight columns over all 777 colleges
Z <- scale(colleges %>% select(-college, -Private))
rownames(Z) <- colleges$college                # keep the names on the rows

# Keep the 30 picked colleges (all in Day 19's elite cluster)
elite <- colleges %>% filter(college %in% picked)
Z_elite <- Z[elite$college, ]
nrow(Z_elite)
```

## Part 1: The Dendrogram (8 minutes)

Fill in the blank to build the tree with complete linkage (see "Hierarchical
clustering in R" on the slides), and remove the `#`s. The plot is drawn
**sideways** so the names fit: the leaves are on the right, and the
**height** of each fusion is on the horizontal axis.

```{r task1, fig.height=7, fig.width=8}
# hc <- hclust(dist(___))
#
# par(mar = c(4, 1, 1, 16))                     # room on the right for the names
# plot(as.dendrogram(hc), horiz = TRUE, xlab = "Height (distance when fused)")
```

*Find Claremont McKenna. Which college does it fuse with first, and at about
what height? Which colleges are in the first group that Harvey Mudd joins?
At about what height do CMC's and Pitzer's branches first meet? And CMC's
and Harvard's? So which is more similar to CMC: Pitzer or Harvard?*

## Part 2: Cutting the Tree (8 minutes)

Cut the tree into 2, 3, and 4 clusters and see where the colleges go at
each cut. Then describe the four clusters. Fill in the three blanks and
remove the `#`s.

```{r task2}
# elite <- elite %>%

#          k4 = cutree(hc, k = ___))
#
# elite %>% count(k2, k3)                       # how the 2 clusters become 3
# elite %>% count(k3, k4)                       # how the 3 clusters become 4
#
# elite %>%
#   group_by(___) %>%                           # one row per cluster
#   summarise(colleges = n(), across(accept_rate:Grad.Rate, mean),
#             share_private = mean(Private == "Yes"))
#
# elite %>% arrange(k4) %>% select(college, k4)  # who is in each cluster
```

*Going from 2 to 3 to 4 clusters, does any cluster ever lose colleges to two
different new clusters, or does one cluster split each time? Give the four
clusters names. Where do the four Claremont Colleges end up? One cluster has
only two colleges: which ones, and what in the averages sets them apart?*

## Part 3: Linkage (6 minutes)

Build the tree three ways and compare the cluster sizes when each is cut
into 4 clusters.

*Predict first, before you run anything: which linkage will give the most
lopsided clusters (one big cluster and a few tiny ones)? Why? (See "Why
single linkage chains".)*

Now fill in the blanks so each column uses the linkage it's named after, and
remove the `#`s.


*Was your prediction right? Which linkage gives the most balanced clusters?
Which colleges does single linkage leave on their own, and why those? Which
linkage would you use to pick peer groups?*

## Bonus (optional)

Work on these if you finish the main questions.

### Bonus 1: Where to cut?

`hc$height` holds the height of every fusion, from the first to the last.

```{r bonus1}
# tail(hc$height, 8)                     # the last 8 fusions
# elite %>% count(h7 = cutree(hc, h = 7))  # cut at height 7
```

*How many clusters does a cut at height 7 give, and why that many? Where is
the biggest gap between two fusion heights, and how many clusters would a
cut inside that gap give?*
